content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper is interested in action recognition, where the accuracy efficiency tradeoff is currently obtained by training multiple models for different clip lengths. The authors argue against the practicality of this approach and propose a single model, Frame Adaptive Network (FAN), that can be trained once and deployed at different clip lenghts. More specifically, the model is composed of three branches, simultaneously trained with long, middle-length and short video clips. The three branches share the same underling weights, that can however be specialized at test time by applying cheap depth-wise convolutions on them to adapt the weights to the clip lenght of inference (weight adaptation). Moreover, the branches feature separate normalization layers (batch norm or layer norm) and a distillation algorithm is imployed, using the long clip branch as the teacher and the other two branches as students. Experiments are conducted on Something-Something V1, Kinetics400 and HMDB51.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- +The paper tackles a clear problem which is a good one to solve, as the current approach of having a spectrum of models trained for different clip lenghts is impractical.
- +The paper illustrates the problem of temporal deviation in detail, comparing to an upper bound given by the use of separate networks. Figure 1 is a very clear illustration of the problem.
- +The proposed model achieves remarkable results. In Tab. 1 it is shown that on Something-SomethingV1 FAN outperforms an ensemble model (basically averaging the predictions of the three branches). I consider this remarkable.
- -the paper is a bit too verbose in some parts: for instance, temporal deviation in section 3 is explained in detail, but it can be easily understood from the introduction of the paper. Also, the batch norm equations in Eq. 1 are not needed and can be assumed known by the ICLR paper reader.
- -I am lukewarm about the idea of weight adaptation. Indeed, the authors argue against the use of separate models for different clip lenghts, and suggest instead to use depthwise convolutions to adapt a single set of weights into time-specific weights. This can be implemented in two ways: i) by precomputing the adapted weights, and collapsing back to the case of different model checkpoints for different timesteps or ii) online adaptation, where the weights are updated on the run. But how can be online computation of adapted weights be faster than its precomputation? In summary, why would be a better idea to adapt the weights against using a separate set of weights? Don't the two solutions collide in practice?
- -The paper lacks a discussion and potential comparison with adaptive models that sample frames dynamically during inference [1,2,3]. Since both this method and those prior works strive for a single model capable of operating at different clip lengths, I think such a discussion is important to have.
- -The authors claim to discover the problem of temporal deviation, meaning the fact that action recognition models do not generalize to different clip length other than the ones they were trained on. I would argue that this problem is known, and it is the reason why the common practice is to train separate models for different clip lengths.
- -Fig. 3 shows how differently batch norm statistics and learnable affine transforms behave at different timesteps. More details are needed about the figure as those values are multi dimensional, and the figure only shows one dimension. How are dimensions collapsed? By mean? or only one is sampled? I wonder what would be the correlation of two different training runs with the sime timesteps. Would we observe a strong correlation under this representation?
- -Two further baselines should be included in the experimental results:
  - A pure distillation baseline where the high clip length model is distilled into models operating on shorter clips. How would that curve behave as compared to ST and FAN? In Eq. 8, this is the type of distillation that is happening. As such, it would be helpful to understand that the overall improvements simply comes from distilling with model with longer clips as a teacher.
  - A single model trained and tested with multiple clip lengths. This would help establishing that simply training a holistic model on all lengths do not work.
- -in Fig. 8, colors of different series are very similar. The authors should consider replacing the figure with a more divergent palette.
- -The "proportional sampling" baseline method is not clear at all and the authors should revise the text explaining it.


[1] Ghodrati, Amir, Babak Ehteshami Bejnordi, and Amirhossein Habibian. "Frameexit: Conditional early exiting for efficient video recognition." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2021.

[2] Wu, Zuxuan, et al. "Adaframe: Adaptive frame selection for fast video recognition." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2019.

[3] Korbar, Bruno, Du Tran, and Lorenzo Torresani. "Scsampler: Sampling salient clips from video for efficient action recognition." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2019.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- C: The paper is fairly clear and well written, with some wordy sentences here and there (e.g. "import to the network" to mean "feed the network"). Sometimes, as discussed above, a lot of text is taken to re-explain concepts or to give unnecessary background.
- Q: Overall the quality of the research is fair. It is a bit difficult for me to understand where the improvements comes from, and adding a couple of baselines as expressed above would help in assessing whether the improved results are coming from trivial techniques such as training on a mixture of clip lengths or by distilling a model trained on longer clips.
- N: The novelty of the paper is not extraordinary, as weight adaptation is the only novel component. Using different normalization layers and distillations sound more like tricks to me than actual technical conributions. The empirical novelty is however good and worth for an empirical paper.
- R: The proposed model is fairly simple and results are probably easy to reproduce given the details provided in the manuscript.
content.summary_of_the_review: In my opinion, this paper represents a borderline submission. The motivation is reasonable and the experimental results are encouraging. However, I don't understand the benefit of using weight adaptation with respect to having separate models. Moreover, some further baselines would understanding the impact of the proposed modules. I'll defer my final judgment after reading the authors' feedback.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the problem of training a single action recognition backbone network, at inference which can switch across the clips of the same video but with different numbers of sampled frames. The authors propose a parallel training framework, called frame adaptive network (FAN), consisting of three basic modules. Specifically, a specialized normalization module to privatize layer-wise normalization parameters for the clips of the same video with different sampled frame numbers; a weight alteration module added to each block of the shared backbone network to privatize extra parameters for the clips of the same video with different sampled frame numbers; and a mutual distillation used to guide the training via transferring the learnt knowledge from the longest clip to all shorter clips. Experiments on four datasets are provided to show the effectiveness of the proposed training framework.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

+ Efficient action recognition model design is critical in real applications.

+ The proposed training framework is easy to understand (but not new).

+  Experiments are conducted with four datasets, including Something-Something V1&V2, large-scale Kinetics-400, and HMDB51.

+ The proposed training framework shows its effectiveness on action recognition networks such as TSM, TEA, SlowFast and Uniformer.

Weaknesses:

-  The method.

This paper lacks of technical novelty.

The motivation, the phenomenon of so called temporal deviation, the ideas of parameter sharing and two core modules (specialized normalization and mutual distillation), and the design of experiments are directly borrowed from existing works for resolution-switchable image classification networks [1-4], especially SAN [1] and RS-Net [2]. 

Beside, the idea of weight alteration is just to add an extra convolutional layer in parallel to each convolutional block of a backbone network, which is also popularly used in many parameter-efficient transfer learning designs, e.g. [5-6]. Moreover, weight alteration increases the depth of a backbone network, which leads to two problems: (1) the depth of a backbone network is increased significantly, and extra parameters are also introduced; (2) experimental comparisons are unfair, as performance improvement should to the modified backbone network but not the original one.

[1] Learning to Learn Parameterized Classification Networks for Scalable Input Images, ECCV 2020.

[2] Resolution Switchable Networks for Runtime Efficient Image Recognition, ECCV 2020.

[3] MutualNet: Adaptive ConvNet via Mutual Learning from Network Width and Resolution, ECCV 2020.

[4] Resolution Adaptive Networks for Efficient Inference, CVPR 2020.

[5] TinyTL: Reduce Memory, Not Parameters for Efficient On-Device Learning, NeurIPS 2020.

[6] Towards a Unified View of Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning, ICLR 2022.

- The motivation.

Although the authors directly use the existing resolution-switchable networks (for image classification tasks) to video based action recognition, and shows its effectiveness, such a motivation is less useful in video based applications, to the best of my knowledge. 

The proposed method, FAN, leads to huge increase/demand of training cost, nearly proportional to the desired clip lengths (e.gl, 8/16/32). As the training for video based action recognition tasks is usually much heavier than image classification, it makes the solution more difficult to use in real applications.

FAN does not generalize well on an unseen sample clip length (e.g., much larger/smaller than the trained ones). In this context, why not directly training the model with the target clip length. 

FAN manually sets the number of sampled clip lengths, so it is not universal.

Note that, in action recognition, top performing networks are mostly based on 3D convolutions. However, 3D networks are not considered in main experiments.

- The experiments.

The design of experiments is heavily borrowed from existing resolution-switchable networks [1-2] for image classifications.

The baseline backbone network should be the original backbone + extra convolutional layers for weight alteration;

Is it possible to apply the proposed FAN to 3D action recognition networks? How about its performance?

If the fusion module of an action recognition network requires a fixed frame length, how to apply the proposed FAN?

I would like to see a comparison of FAN with slimmable neural network design (Yu, et al., ICLR 2018) with the largest clip length. This is important to show the advantage of FAN.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The presentation is mostly clear. However this work suffers from low novelty. It is hard to implement in real applications. No code is provided.

Please refer to my comments in 'Strength And Weaknesses' for details.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper is below the acceptance bar of ICLR. 

Please refer to my comments in 'Strength And Weaknesses' for details.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The performance of traditional networks will drop a lot when the testing and training number of frames are different. Motivated by this, this paper proposed a method to train a video network that can do inference at different input number of frames. The method consists of three components, specialized normalization, which assigns different normalization layers to different input; weight alteration, which changes the weights of each block to fit different input; mutual distillation, which improves over standard CE loss. The method is evaluated on different action recognition datasets and several backbones.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
1. The paper is easy to follow.
2. The proposed weight alteration is an interesting method to adapt the model to different inputs.
3. The method is evaluated on mutiple datasets and backbones.

Weakness

My first concern is that I don't think there are many technical contributions in this paper.

1. The frame adaptive network has been studied in [1], where the author feed different number of frames (also with different resolutions) to the network and train it with a similar mutual distillation. The author should have a more detailed discussion with this paper.
2. The temporal deviation seems to be straightforward to me, since many works have shown that networks cannot generalize to different resolutions well at inference time.
3. The normalization shifting problem has also been studied in [2], and the proposed specialized normalization is the same as the private BN in [2].
4. The mutual distillation is the same as in [1].

My second concern is that the results are not very strong and seems not very convincing to me.
1. Some results of previous methods seem to be lower than that reported in the original paper. For example, Uniformer-S 16-frame has a performance of 53.8. But in Figure 6(d), Uniformer only has a performance slightly higher than 50. For all the results reported in the paper, do the authors cite them from the original paper or reproduced them?
2. I would suggest the author to conduct more experiments on slowfast and uniformer backbone on different datasets, because these are stronger baselines. TSM seems to be a weak baseline on these datasets.

Some minor comments
1. In Fig.3, what is index in the figure.
2. There should be more discussion about adaptive/anytime networks in the related work. Below are some references, but there should be more.
(1) AR-Net: Adaptive Frame Resolution for Efficient Action Recognition
(2) AdaFuse: Adaptive Temporal Fusion Network for Efficient Action Recognition

References

[1] Yang, Taojiannan, et al. "MutualNet: Adaptive ConvNet via Mutual Learning from Different Model Configurations." IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (2021).

[2] Slimmable neural networks. ICLR 2019.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The proposed method is clearly introduced. But I don't think there are many technical contributions as explained in the weakness part.
content.summary_of_the_review: I don't think there are many technical contributions as explained in the weakness part, and the experimental results are not strong and convincing to me.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes frame adaptive networks (FAN) for video classification that can adapt to different clip lengths at test time. FAN consists of three components: Specialized normalization which uses different normalization layers for each frame size; weight alteration which learns a task-specific depthwise convolution layer in each encoder block; and mutual distillation to transfer knowledge from  high-resolution to low-resolution branches. In experiments, the resulting system achieves higher accuracy and consistency across three different clip length settings, when compared to baselines of training individual networks for each clip length, or training a single network with mixed input lengths.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Pros
- The paper studies an important problem in video recognition, which has received limited attention as mainstream models require a fixed input clip length.  
- The overall design of FAN is simple and intuitive. It is a good idea to share the majority of computation throughout the network, and use a small number of parameters to adapt to different frame rates.  
- Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms baselines when tested with different clip lengths.  

## Cons
- I feel that FAN consists of little technical novelty on top existing work on adapter modules for transfer/multi-task learning. Training with shared backbone and task-specific normalization and depthwise convolution have been shown effective at saving parameters while improving performance over individual tasks (e.g. [a, b]), and knowledge distillation is commonly used to improve the consistency between outputs of multiple network branches. There should probably be more discussion of these related areas, and the relation between FAN and prior approaches.  
	- [a] Learning multiple visual domains with residual adapters. Rebuffi et al., NeurIPS'17  
	- [b] Depthwise Convolution Is All You Need for Learning Multiple Visual Domains. Guo et al., AAAI'19  
- The main contribution of FAN to me is the formulation of adaptive frame classification as a multidomain learning problem, though it does not fully address the problem of predicting inputs at arbitrary input lengths. It is true that interpolating between training frame numbers (4-8-16) works substantially better on FAN on baseline, but as the range of frame length becomes larger (say 4 to 128) I suspect more than three branches will be added to maintain a good performance across the board. The authors may consider dynamic convolutions (e.g. [c]) as an alternative, where the kernel weights automatically adapts to the input data.  
	- [c] Dynamic Convolution: Attention over Convolution Kernels. Chen et al., CVPR'20
- Apart from the ablations on FAN, I would have liked to see more analysis on the problem of frame-adaptive recognition itself, comparing the results across model families. From my experience, for instance, models heavily focused on spatial modeling (e.g. TSN) performs more consistent when evaluated with different number of frames, while those more sensitive to temporal cues suffer heavily when clip length is altered. There should also be simple baselines of training on smaller number of frames, then evaluating on longer input clips using a sliding window with mean pooling, which is common practice of training on action recognition datasets like Kinetics.
- From figure 9 weight alteration seems to only make a marginal impact on model performance. I wonder if this difference stems from the extra modeling capacity from the depthwise convolution layers?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity of the paper is good. The writing is easy to follow and the proposed method is presented with detailed equations and figures, which should make it easier to reproduce the experimental results.
I am more concerned about the technical novelty of the work, as it shares many similarities to prior work on domain adaptation and multitask learning.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think the paper makes an attempt at the challenging problem of frame-adaptive video recognition, with mostly positive experimental results. However, l feel that the paper still needs more work on demonstrating its technical contributions in the context of prior works, refining the approach for inputs of arbitrary input lengths, and further experimental studies on the nature of the problem itself. Therefore I set my initial rating at (weak) reject but look forward to the authors' responses to my concerns.
